extracted.intended_audience: artisans, engineers, and readers interested in manufacturing and replication processes
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptions and practical guidance for a wide range of mechanical copying/replication methods used in manufactures (moulding, stamping, punching, drawing, engraving, turning, etc.), including when each method is appropriate and key process considerations. Aimed at explaining how to produce uniform or multiplied copies of objects in different materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moulding complex earthenware
rubrics_metrics.description: The embossed ornaments, polygonal shape, fluted surfaces, and other features of many earthenware pieces are difficult or costly by hand but become easy and uniform when made by pressing the soft material into a hard mould.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care and skill in preparing the mould are repaid by the multitude it produces; use moulding to make complex, repeated shapes cheaply and uniformly. Example: upper surface moulded while underside is lathe-figured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial moulding with lathe finishing
rubrics_metrics.description: In many china-manufactory works, one part only of the article is moulded (e.g. upper surface of a plate) while the under side is finished by the lathe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine moulding and turning to balance economy with functional/finish requirements; mould ornamental parts and turn structural or mating surfaces as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glass seals copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Colored glass rod is heated until soft, pinched between brass nippers one side of which bears the device to produce a seal, producing imitations that can be multiplied cheaply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper heating of the glass and a well-finished mould are necessary to produce acceptable imitations. Note the limits: such seals become common and cheap (example: threepence a dozen at Birmingham).

rubrics_metrics.name: Square glass bottles production in moulds
rubrics_metrics.description: Round unfinished blown bottle is placed while soft into a two-part iron or copper mould (used hot), then closed and blown strongly so the glass is forced against the mould sides to achieve square form and identical capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heated two-part moulds engraved inside (to imprint maker's name) and strong blowing to ensure exact capacity and consistent imprinting across many bottles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wooden snuff-boxes moulding
rubrics_metrics.description: Wood or horn is softened by long boiling in water and, while soft, forced into iron or steel moulds cut with the requisite patterns and exposed to great pressure until dry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soften material sufficiently before moulding and maintain pressure until dry to retain embossed patterns; suitable for producing imitations at low cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horn moulding for handles and ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Horn softens with water and heat and can be pressed into moulds to become embossed in relief and formed into various shapes (straightened, bent) suitable for knife- and umbrella-handles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit horn's thermoplastic properties for repeated decorative/functional parts; moulding multiplies shapes cheaply and in endless variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited moulding of tortoiseshell
rubrics_metrics.description: The same moulding principle applies to tortoiseshell, but due to the higher price of raw material, moulding is less often used and carvings are usually performed by hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hand carving for high-value materials when demand for carved pieces is low; weigh material cost against economies of moulding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tobacco pipe-making in two-part iron moulds
rubrics_metrics.description: Pipes are formed in iron two-part moulds each embracing one half of the stem; the bore hole is formed by thrusting a wire through clay while enclosed in the mould. Moulds may bear sunk figures or names producing relief on finished pipes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two-part moulds and internal wire cores to produce consistent shapes and bores; mould design can incorporate makers' marks in relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embossing calico by engraved rollers
rubrics_metrics.description: Calico is embossed by passing it through rollers, one engraved (in intaglio) with the pattern; the cloth is pressed into the cavities and preserves its figured appearance after considerable use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roller engraving enables all-over raised patterns; ensure roller pattern is correctly formed and pressure is sufficient to force cloth into cavities for durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embossing leather by rollers
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar to calico embossing: leather is forced into engraved roller cavities; parts not opposite cavities are powerfully condensed between rollers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use high pressure rollers and appropriate cavity design to emboss leather reliably; expect condensation and thickness changes in non-embossed areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swaging for metal forming
rubrics_metrics.description: Smiths use paired steel blocks (swages) with sunk cavities; heated iron rod ends are upset and placed in swages, then struck repeatedly (often with rotation) so softened metal assumes mould form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat and upsetting are prerequisites; strike with controlled blows and turn work quarter rounds to form symmetric heads and rims; swaging is effective for producing repeated shapes like bolt heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engraving by pressure (Perkins' method) for mass replication
rubrics_metrics.description: An engraving is cut in soft steel, hardened without injury; a soft-steel cylinder is pressed with great force and rolled over it to receive the design in relief, hardened, then used to print thousands of perfect facsimiles on copper plates via successive rolling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This chain (original engraving → hardened roller → plates → hardened intermediates → further rollers) multiplies impressions almost indefinitely. Two principles help prevent forgery (perfect identity of impressions and ability to employ eminent artists for a single original), but the same principle also enables wide forgery if exploited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgery vulnerability from copying processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of copying (rollers, transfers) furnishes expedients for imitating engravings or printed patterns however complicated; suggested methods include transferring ink from a note to a stone or elastic medium, then printing from that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that advanced copying can make near-perfect facsimiles; anti-forgery measures must consider transferability of ink and repeatability of impressions. Examples and conjectures (use of solvents, porous porcelain, elastic glue-and-treacle sheets, india-rubber membranes) are discussed as potential forgery routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold and silver moulding by rollers
rubrics_metrics.description: Thin slips of metal receive form by passing between steel rollers on which the pattern is embossed or engraved, taking successive copies of the device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roller embossing is effective for thin sheet metal ornamentation; ensure roller engraving quality to transfer fine details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of ornamental papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Sheets of paper coloured or covered with gold/silver leaf and embossed with patterns are produced by passing them between engraved rollers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use engraved rollers designed for the desired pattern and gilding processes; roller quality affects sharpness and repeatability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stamping via large screw-presses
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying by stamping is executed by large screw-presses (screw and heavy fly-wheel), typically on metals, sometimes when hot or in a pasty state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select appropriate press (manual, water, or steam-powered) and coordinate temperature/state of metal for sharp impressions; stamping suits coinage, medals, and heavy ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coin and medal striking processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Coins produced by screw-presses; medals require multiple blows and annealing cycles because the first blow hardens and makes subsequent blows injurious; large medals may require many repetitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect to anneal between strikes and to repeat pressing processes many times for large or high-relief medals to avoid die/metal damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stamping ornaments for accoutrements and furniture
rubrics_metrics.description: Brass ornaments are stamped up out of solid or sheet brass by placing between dies and allowing a heavy weight to drop from five to fifteen feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate die geometry and drop weight to form brass ornaments; process is suited to high-throughput production of ornamental parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buttons and nail-heads formed by dies
rubrics_metrics.description: Buttons embossed with crests and various hemispherical or polyhedral nail-heads are produced by dies and stamping methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Die design determines final shape; use stamping for consistent volume production of small decorative hardware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clichée (pasty-alloy stamping) process
rubrics_metrics.description: A semi-molten alloy (lead/tin/antimony) in a pasty state is placed under a die and driven with force into the finest lines; the result is admirably sharp but ragged at the sides and requires trimming and lathe-equalizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ for sharp relief work where post-process trimming and turning are acceptable; expect edge raggedness and need for finishing operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punching to cut repeated apertures
rubrics_metrics.description: Driving a steel punch by blow or pressure through a substance to cut repeated apertures; sometimes the punched-out part is discarded, other times it is the desired product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use punches for mass production of uniform apertures or tokens; coordinate punch size, press type, and material thickness for intended output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punching iron plate for boilers (specifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Steel punch diameters from three-eighths to three-quarters of an inch drive out circular discs from plates one-quarter to five-eighths inch thick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose punch diameter and technical parameters matched to plate thickness; punching iron plate for boilers requires heavy-duty punches and presses.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-density perforation of tinned iron and copper
rubrics_metrics.description: Sheets of tinned/japanned ware and copper are perforated with extremely small holes in great multitudes (examples: plates with >3000 holes per square inch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialized screw-press punching trades exist for such precision/performance; ensure tooling and presses can produce regular, high-density perforations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buhl (inlaid brass and rosewood) formed by punching
rubrics_metrics.description: Inlaid plates (buhl work) are formed by punching; both the cut-out parts and the remaining parts are often employed in the inlay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punching can create both the inlaid motif and the insert; coordinate dimensions and tolerances for proper fit in furniture ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cards for guns produced by punches
rubrics_metrics.description: Thin card discs are cut by small steel tools that produce innumerable circles each precisely fitting the bore for which designed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accurate punches sized to barrel bores to produce uniform ammunition cards at scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornaments of gilt paper cut by punches
rubrics_metrics.description: Golden stars, leaves, and devices for ornamenting paper goods are cut out of gilt paper sheets by various shaped punches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punch selection and die maintenance are key to producing delicate gilt paper ornament affordably and rapidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steel chain link uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch/clock chains consist of small sheet-steel pieces; it is crucial that each piece be exactly the same size and holes for rivets be placed at correct equal distances so the chain remains straight and fit for purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain tight dimensional tolerances on link plates and precise hole placement; small deviations render the chain unfit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying with elongation — wire drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Metal is made cylindrical and drawn through circular holes in steel plates; at each passage it becomes smaller, and its section copies the last hole it passed through; imperfections in draw-plate holes produce longitudinal lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use successive draw-plates to achieve target diameter and cross-section (square, half-round, star-shaped pinion wire); expect and remediate surface lines from hole imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tube drawing using triblets
rubrics_metrics.description: For tubes where internal diameter must be uniform, a succession of steel cylinders (triblets) is drawn through the brass tube while the tube is itself drawn through holes to reduce outside diameter; withdrawal of triblet leaves polished internal surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine external hole drawing and internal triblet drawing to meet both internal and external dimensional requirements, e.g. telescope tubes; expect considerable elongation (sometimes double length).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaden water pipes by drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaden pipes formerly cast but now drawn by forcing an iron triblet into a cast cylinder with a central hole and drawing through a series of holes until desired thickness and extension achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace casting with drawing for cheaper and better pipes; use long triblets and staged draw-plates for controlled wall thickness and length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iron rolling into profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Cylinders of iron thicker than wire are formed by passing wrought iron between rollers each with a semi-cylindrical groove; bar iron is shaped into round, square, half-round, oval, etc., with longitudinal lines due to imperfect roller contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design roller grooves to match desired cross-sections; expect longitudinal marks from imperfect roller contact and plan finishing as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable-thickness rolling (rail profiles)
rubrics_metrics.description: When non-uniform thickness is required (e.g. rails with deeper middle), the groove in rollers is cut deeper where additional strength is needed so the produced iron matches intended shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engineer roller grooves to create targeted cross-sectional variation; this produces functional profiles tailored to load/support geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vermicelli and paste extrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Paste forms (vermicelli, pastry ornaments, confectionery lozenges) are made by forcing material through holes in tin plate, producing strings or shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrusion through appropriately shaped holes yields consistent decorative/food shapes; same method applies across culinary and confectionery uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pentagraph for copying drawings/maps (altered dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pentagraph copies drawings or maps and is usually used for reduction but can enlarge; it mechanically links a tracing point to a drawing implement to produce scaled copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pentagraphs to produce scaled reproductions; suitable for drawings, maps, and regulating automated profile-drawing mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying by turning and mandril accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning on a mandril involves a steel axis supporting the work; all work executed partakes of the mandril's irregularities and perfect circularity requires equal accuracy in mandril and its collar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure mandril and collar precision to achieve circularity and dimensional accuracy in turned parts; use appropriate chucks and support bearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rose engine-turning for repeated patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Rose engine-turning uses rosettes or patterned circular plates on the mandril that force the cutting tool to trace the same pattern on the work, usually producing diminished copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ rosettes to generate intricate repeating patterns; expect scale reduction based on cutter distance relative to rosette radius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying dies with a lathe (scaling effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lathe copies dies by carrying a blunt tracing point in a slow spiral over the die while a linked cutting point cuts the face of soft steel on the same or diminished scale; excellence increases as copy is smaller than original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use die-copying lathes to prepare coarse features and leave finer lines to manual artists; reducing scale can mask imperfections and yield tolerable smaller-scale dies (e.g. crown-piece die to sixpence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine shoe-last copying (adjustable scaling and mirroring)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern last placed in the apparatus guides cutting of two pieces of wood adjusted by screws; inserting a reversing wheel between pieces can produce a mirrored (left) last from a right-foot pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machine enables production of lasts of different sizes and mirrored counterparts by mechanical adjustment; use screw adjustments and reversing wheels for scale and handedness control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engines for copying busts and statues
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical engines (Watt, Hawkins) have been constructed to produce copies of busts or statues at same or reduced size in various materials (ivory, etc.); sometimes combined with casting to make acquisition cheaper and diffuse works widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use copying engines to multiply sculptural works at different scales; pair with casting for economical distribution, but be aware mechanisms and materials affect fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screw-cutting as copying operation (thread count vs form independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Screw-cutting by a lathe with a screw on the mandril copies the number of threads in a given length, but form, length, and diameter of the produced screw can be independent; alternative method uses a pattern screw connected by wheels to guide cutting point, producing scaled/coarsened threads depending on relative mandril speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose method based on whether exact thread pitch replication or scaled adjustment is desired; expect defects in original to be transmitted under modified circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing from copper-plates with altered dimensions (Gonord's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Paris watchmaker produced impressions from the same copper-plate at different sizes (larger or smaller) by methods not published; conjectured mechanisms include transferring ink to a fluid or elastic sheet (glue-and-treacle or india-rubber), stretching or relaxing it, then re-transferring to paper; alternative approach transfers design to stone for lithographic printing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To alter linear scale of transfer prints, consider intermediate elastic or fluid surfaces that can be expanded/contracted before re-transfer or use transfer to stone and lithography. Note practical difficulties: uniform scaling, ink transferability, time, and repeatability; observed evidence (identical line sets across sizes, ink quantity differences) supports feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine producing engraving from medals (tracing-to-diamond transfer)
rubrics_metrics.description: An instrument fixes a medal and a copper at right angles on sliding plates; a bar carries a tracing-point touching the medal and a diamond-point touching the copper-plate such that movements of the tracing-point cause the diamond to draw corresponding sections on the copper (a section through the medal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mechanically linked tracing and diamond points with coordinated slides to render relief objects into engraved copper sections; suitable for converting medals and reliefs into plate engravings.
